title: Similarity & Scale Factors
coreInsight: Similar figures preserve shape and corresponding angles while every corresponding length scales by one factor; areas therefore scale by the square of that factor.
targetLearnerRealization: One multiplicative factor controls all corresponding lengths of similar figures, while two-dimensional coverage scales by the square of that factor.
learningObjectives: Identify a common scale factor across corresponding lengths.
Match corresponding sides by position and angle structure rather than arbitrary size order.
Explain why perimeter scales by k and area by k².
Use area ratios inside nested similar figures.

continuity.openingCallback: Apply one ratio's multiplicative batch to every length of a whole figure while preserving its angle pattern.
closingSeeds: Scaled figures can hide inside coordinate, circle, and area-decomposition problems.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Scaling is additive rather than multiplicative.
Corresponding sides can be paired arbitrarily.
Area scales by the same factor as length.
Similarity and congruence are the same relation.

beats.purpose: Transfer proportional batch reasoning to every side of one shape.
beats.expectedRealization: A single factor of 2 multiplies all corresponding lengths; adding a fixed amount does not preserve shape.
beats.transitionIn: A ratio preserved a labeled comparison by multiplying both quantities by one factor. Let that factor act on every side of a triangle at once.
beats.whyNow: The contrast exposes additive scaling before similarity vocabulary appears.
beats.entryBridge: Compare each new side with its corresponding original side.
beats.exitBridge: Three lengths 3, 4, 5 become 6, 8, 10 under one factor of 2.
learnerPrompts: Which new side set applies the same multiplier to all three sides?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Every side doubles, so the triangle keeps its shape.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute new ÷ original for each corresponding side; all three ratios must match.

visual.ariaLabel: Triangle side lengths three four five scaled by two to six eight ten

steps.body: 6/3 = 8/4 = 10/5 = 2. One multiplier acts on all corresponding lengths.

resolution.takeaway: Similarity uses one multiplicative scale factor, not one added amount.

beats.purpose: Make correspondence depend on angle and adjacency structure.
beats.expectedRealization: Sides correspond when they occupy the same role between matching angles.
beats.transitionIn: The factor works only after the correct side pairs are identified.
beats.prompt: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR, with A matching P, B matching Q, and C matching R. Which side corresponds to AC?

options.text: Any side with a convenient length

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. AC joins the first and third matched vertices, as PR does.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Carry both endpoints through the stated vertex matching: A→P and C→R.

steps.body: AB↔PQ, BC↔QR, and AC↔PR. The vertex order preserves which angles bound each side.

resolution.takeaway: Match roles first; calculate ratios second.

beats.purpose: Derive squared area scaling from two independent dimensions.
beats.expectedRealization: Scaling both length and width by k creates k rows of k copies, hence k² area.
beats.transitionIn: A factor of 2 doubles every boundary length. Now count what happens across both directions of a tiled square.
beats.prompt: A 3-by-3 square is scaled by factor 2 to a 6-by-6 square. By what factor does its area grow?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Twice as many rows and twice as many columns make four times the tiles.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare 6×6 with 3×3, or count the multiplier in both dimensions.

steps.title: Compare coverage
steps.body: Original area is 9; scaled area is 36. The ratio 36/9 = 4 = 2².

resolution.takeaway: Length scales by k; area scales by k².

beats.purpose: Separate same-shape similarity from same-size congruence.
beats.expectedRealization: Congruence is similarity with scale factor 1.
beats.transitionIn: The 3-by-3 and 6-by-6 squares share shape but not size.
beats.prompt: Which statement is true about two figures with equal corresponding angles and scale factor 3?

options.text: They are similar but not congruent.
They are congruent because their angles match.
They are neither similar nor congruent.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Same shape gives similarity; scale factor 3 changes size, so not congruent.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Congruent figures require corresponding lengths to match, which means scale factor 1.

steps.body: Similarity preserves shape and permits resizing. Congruence preserves both shape and size.

resolution.takeaway: Congruence is the scale-factor-1 case of similarity.

beats.purpose: Name similarity and its length/area consequences after discovery.
beats.expectedRealization: Correspondence and a common multiplier organize all measurements.
beats.name: Similarity and scale factor
beats.conciseDefinition: Similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding lengths. If each length is multiplied by k, perimeter is multiplied by k and area by k².
beats.formalization: new length/original length = k · P_new = kP · A_new = k²A
beats.memoryHook: Match first; one factor for lengths, its square for area.

beats.purpose: Apply linear scaling and area decomposition in a contest grid.
beats.expectedRealization: Tripling width and height multiplies area by 9; the kite and corner waste each occupy half the bounding rectangle.
beats.transitionIn: Set the scale factor to 3. Both grid dimensions triple, so square-unit coverage must respond twice.
beats.whyNow: The learner has separated k from k² and can coordinate scaling with familiar area decomposition.
beats.entryBridge: Scale the bounding dimensions, find its area, then use the kite's half-rectangle relationship.
beats.exitBridge: The 18-by-21 rectangle has area 378; its four corner pieces occupy half, or 189.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A shape and bounding grid controlled by one scale factor.
learnerPrompts: What are the large grid dimensions?
Why is multiplying the small area only by 3 incorrect?
What is the bounding rectangle's area?
Why do the four corner pieces occupy half?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The waste is half of 18×21, or 189 square inches.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Tripling both dimensions multiplies area by 9; then compare the kite with its bounding rectangle.

steps.title: Measure coverage
steps.body: The rectangle area is 18×21 = 378 square inches.

steps.title: Use decomposition
steps.body: The kite occupies half the rectangle, so the four corner pieces occupy the other half: 378/2 = 189.

resolution.takeaway: A length factor acts once in each dimension, so area receives the factor twice.

beats.purpose: Use squared scale and equal partition inside nested similar triangles.
beats.expectedRealization: Side ratio 2:3 creates inner-to-outer area 4:9; the remaining 5 units split among three congruent trapezoids.
beats.transitionIn: A rectangular grid made the squared factor visible. Now use unit equilateral triangles inside a less obvious scaled figure.
beats.whyNow: The learner can combine area ratios with G4's complement and equal-piece reasoning.
beats.entryBridge: Treat outer side 3 and inner side 2, square those counts, subtract the ring, then share it equally.
beats.exitBridge: One trapezoid has area 5/3 units compared with inner area 4, giving 5:12.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Similar figures tiled into unit regions with a remaining ring.
learnerPrompts: Why are the three trapezoids congruent?
How do side counts 3 and 2 become area counts 9 and 4?
How much area remains in the ring?
What is one trapezoid's ratio to the inner triangle?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. One trapezoid to the inner triangle is 5/3:4 = 5:12.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Square the 2:3 side ratio, subtract inner from outer, then divide the ring equally among three pieces.

steps.title: Square the side scale
steps.body: Outer and inner areas are in ratio 3²:2² = 9:4.

steps.title: Find and share the ring
steps.body: The ring has 9−4 = 5 area units, so each congruent trapezoid has 5/3.

resolution.takeaway: Square the length ratio before subtracting or sharing areas.

beats.whyNow: Return to a direct length ratio after layered area work.
beats.entryBridge: Find the multiplier from the known pair and apply it to the corresponding side.
learnerPrompts: Which known corresponding pair reveals k?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use 10/4 = 2.5, then multiply the corresponding 6 by 2.5.

resolution.takeaway: One factor must fit every corresponding length.

beats.purpose: Assess vertex-order correspondence before ratio calculation.
beats.whyNow: Make pairing, not arithmetic, the critical step.
beats.entryBridge: Translate both endpoints through the similarity statement.
beats.exitBridge: DE corresponds to XY and scales from 7 to 21.
learnerPrompts: Which vertices match D and E?
beats.incorrectFeedback: From triangle DEF similar to XYZ, D→X and E→Y, so DE↔XY.

steps.body: DE corresponds to XY. Since EF=5 corresponds to YZ=15, k=3; therefore XY=3(7)=21.

resolution.takeaway: Correspondence determines which ratio is meaningful.

beats.whyNow: Test k² without a grid animation.
beats.entryBridge: Square the linear factor before multiplying area.
learnerPrompts: How many dimensions receive the factor 4?

resolution.takeaway: Area records scaling in two dimensions.

beats.purpose: Assess the boundary between similarity and congruence.
beats.whyNow: Use a scale factor below 1 to prevent size-order cues.
beats.exitBridge: Factor 1/2 preserves shape but changes size.
learnerPrompts: Does every corresponding length stay equal?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The figures are similar but not congruent.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Congruence requires k=1; k=1/2 changes every length.

steps.body: Equal corresponding angles and one common factor give similarity. Because 1/2≠1, corresponding lengths differ, so the figures are not congruent.

resolution.takeaway: Similarity permits resizing; congruence does not.

beats.purpose: Assess simultaneous linear and area consequences.
beats.whyNow: Finish by coordinating two measurement dimensions.
beats.entryBridge: Apply k to boundary and k² to coverage.
beats.exitBridge: At k=3/2, perimeter becomes 45 and area becomes 180.
learnerPrompts: Which quantity receives one factor and which receives two?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The new perimeter is 45 and area is 180.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiply perimeter by 3/2 and area by (3/2)².

resolution.takeaway: Dimension decides the exponent on the scale factor.

beats.purpose: Consolidate correspondence, factor, conditions, and measurement dimension.
beats.expectedRealization: Similarity problems become systematic when roles precede ratios.
beats.transitionIn: Triangles, grids, kites, perimeters, and nested regions all obeyed the same scaling controls.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable similarity routine? Select all four.

options.text: Match vertices, angles, and sides by role.
Find one common multiplicative length factor.
Check the same factor fits every corresponding length.
Use k for lengths and perimeter, k² for area.

response.feedback: Each action protects the scale relationship.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Match, find, verify, then use the correct dimensional power.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four matter; an unverified or mismatched ratio cannot establish similarity.

steps.body: Correspondence tells what to compare; the common factor establishes similarity; dimension determines how derived measures scale.

resolution.takeaway: Match first, scale consistently, square the factor for area.

beats.purpose: Consolidate transfer to hidden similar subfigures.
beats.expectedRealization: A useful similar figure may appear only after adding an altitude, parallel line, or enclosing shape.
beats.transitionIn: The scale factor was visible in one grid and hidden inside nested triangles.
beats.prompt: What extra line or enclosing shape could expose corresponding lengths when two similar figures are hidden inside a larger diagram?
beats.takeaway: When similarity is hidden, construct a line that makes matching angles and sides visible.

notes: Design: F3's common multiplier expands from paired quantities to every corresponding side. Correspondence is secured before ratios, a tiled square derives k² area growth, and congruence is separated as k=1. Authentic problems combine scaling with decomposition and nested area ratios.

Beat outline: whole-shape scaling -> correspondence -> area growth -> similarity/congruence -> name -> authentic kite -> authentic triangle ring -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> hidden-scale reflection.
Both mapped animations are referenced unchanged after submission over their full timelines. Existing generic choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer or animation source changes were made.

Generated results were verified through corresponding ratios, squared scale factors, and direct perimeter/area recomputation, with independent fraction simplification or option audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
